client: I've been really struggling since my grandmother passed away last month. Every time there's a family get-together, I just can't seem to enjoy it — all I can think about is that she's not there, and it makes the whole thing feel hollow and almost painful to be around everyone. I'm not even sure talking about it is going to change how I feel, but I figured I'd try.
therapist: I'm really glad you decided to reach out, and I want you to know that what you're carrying — this grief that shows up even in moments that are supposed to feel warm — makes complete sense. I notice that even as you're describing all of this, there's something very quiet and subdued in the way you're sharing it, almost like part of you is holding back or feeling a little numb, which can sometimes happen when we're exhausted from grieving. I'm curious — when you say you're not sure talking will change anything, does that feel more like hopelessness, or is it something closer to feeling like the pain is just too big to put into words?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: Honestly, it's probably a bit of both. There's this part of me that feels like no matter what I say out loud, she's still going to be gone when I leave here, and that's not something words can fix. But I think you're right that I'm holding back — it's like if I actually let myself say how much it hurts, it becomes more real somehow, and I'm not sure I'm ready for that.
therapist: What you just said takes a lot of self-awareness — recognizing that keeping the pain at a distance feels like a way of protecting yourself from it becoming fully real. That instinct makes so much sense, because letting grief in fully can feel like losing her all over again. I'm wondering, at your own pace, what's one small thing about her that you'd be willing to let yourself say out loud today?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: She used to call me every Sunday morning, just to check in, and she'd always ask what I'd eaten that week like she was still worried I wasn't taking care of myself. It sounds so small when I say it out loud, but those calls were kind of the one thing I could count on, and now Sunday mornings feel like this weird empty space I don't know what to do with. I didn't realize until just now how much I miss just... being someone she checked on.
therapist: That doesn't sound small at all — that weekly call was a thread of consistent love and care, and what you just named, *being someone she checked on*, speaks to something really deep about feeling seen and held by her. There's something tender in the quiet, careful way you're sharing this, like you're handling something precious. I want to gently ask — now that you've let yourself say it out loud, what does it feel like to have named that loss?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, moderate-paced speech

client: It feels a little like I poked a bruise — like now that I've said it, there's this dull ache sitting right in the middle of my chest that wasn't quite as loud before. I think part of me wanted to keep it vague so it wouldn't hurt this specifically. But I guess there's also something almost... relieving about it, like I've been carrying this unnamed thing around and now it at least has a shape.
therapist: That image of giving something a shape is really beautiful, and it points to something important in how we process grief — the unnamed things we carry can actually weigh more than the ones we've faced directly. I notice you're speaking quickly, like there's a lot moving through you right now, and I just want to invite you to take a breath and let yourself sit with what you just discovered. What does it feel like to know that the ache has a shape now — does it feel like something you can begin to be with, even a little?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: Maybe a little, but I'm also not sure "being with it" is something I actually know how to do — like, what does that even look like in practice? When Sunday comes around and my phone doesn't ring, I don't think I'm going to be able to just sit quietly and feel my feelings, I'm more likely to just find something to distract myself with. I want to believe it helps to have named it, but I'm honestly not sure that changes what happens when I'm actually in those moments.
therapist: That's such an honest and grounded question, and you're right that naming something doesn't automatically change what we do in the hard moments — the distraction instinct is real and it makes sense. But I want to offer a gentle reframe: what if, on a Sunday morning when the phone doesn't ring, instead of trying to *sit with* the feeling perfectly, you did something small that honored her — like eating something she would have asked about, and noticing that? Sometimes "being with grief" doesn't have to look like stillness; it can look like a tiny, intentional moment of remembering.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: That's actually not as impossible-sounding as I expected, but I'm also a little worried it could just make me sadder — like, what if I make her favorite thing and it just reminds me she's not there to ask about it, and I end up feeling worse than if I'd just distracted myself? I don't want to turn Sunday mornings into something I dread even more than I already do. I guess I'm just not sure I trust myself to handle whatever comes up if I actually lean into it instead of away from it.
therapist: The worry you're describing — that leaning in might leave you worse off than leaning away — is really common, and it actually tells me something important: that you've been protecting yourself carefully, and that protection has felt necessary. I want to gently reflect that even as you're raising all these concerns, your voice sounds quite soft and a little rushed, like there's a lot of anxious thinking happening underneath, which makes me wonder if part of you is already bracing for Sunday before it's even arrived. What if we started even smaller — not with her favorite food, but just with noticing the moment when the silence hits, and giving yourself permission to feel whatever comes without any pressure to handle it a certain way?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, soft-spoken, very rapid speech

client: I think "no pressure to handle it a certain way" is the part that actually makes that feel more doable, because usually I'm already judging myself for not grieving the right way or feeling guilty that I'm not thinking about her enough, or sometimes guilty that I am and it's making me useless for the rest of the day. But I'm still a little skeptical, because "just noticing" sounds simple and I have a feeling in the moment it won't feel simple at all. I guess I'm willing to try, but I want to be honest that I'm not very confident it won't just spiral into me feeling worse and more alone than before.
therapist: The way you're talking right now — very fast, with a kind of urgency underneath — makes me wonder if even describing this is stirring up more than your words are letting on, like your body might already be feeling the weight of what you're anticipating. And what you named about the guilt — judging yourself for grieving too much *or* too little — that's actually a really important thing to hold onto, because that self-criticism is often what turns a manageable moment of sadness into a spiral. So perhaps the real practice for Sunday isn't just noticing the silence, but also noticing when that judging voice shows up, and gently reminding yourself that there is no "right" way to miss someone you loved this much.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, very rapid speech

client: That actually landed differently than I expected — the part about the judging voice being what turns it into a spiral, because I think that's true and I've never quite connected those two things before. But I'm also sitting here wondering how I'm supposed to catch that voice in the moment when it's so automatic, like it's just part of how I think and I don't even notice it until I'm already deep in the guilt. I want to believe I can do that, but it feels a bit like being told to notice when you're already underwater.
therapist: That underwater image is so apt, and it actually points to exactly why we don't start by trying to catch the voice mid-spiral — we start by noticing it in quieter moments first, so it becomes more familiar and recognizable before the hard ones hit. I'm also struck by something in the way you're speaking right now — there's a kind of energy and aliveness in your voice that feels a little different from where we started, almost like something has shifted even as you're describing the difficulty. I'm curious whether you notice that too — because sometimes the moment a new idea actually lands, something in us responds before our skeptical mind has a chance to talk us out of it.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, fast speech

client: I hate to admit it, but yeah, something does feel a little different — like there's slightly more air in the room than when I walked in, even though nothing about the situation has actually changed. I think part of me is suspicious of that feeling, like I'm worried I'll leave here feeling okay and then Sunday will come and knock me flat anyway. But maybe that's just the judging voice doing its thing again, already trying to talk me out of something before I've even tried it.
therapist: You just caught the judging voice in real time — that's not a small thing, and it's exactly the kind of noticing we were just talking about. There's something really meaningful in the fact that you can already feel the difference between "something shifted" and the part of you that immediately wants to brace against it. What if you let yourself take that "more air in the room" feeling with you, not as a promise that Sunday will be easy, but as evidence that you're more capable of moving through this than you've been giving yourself credit for?
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, moderate volume, moderate-paced speech

client: I think that's the part I struggle with most — believing I'm capable of handling it, because my track record lately feels like a lot of falling apart at family dinners and avoiding phone calls from people who want to check in on me. But I notice I'm already trying to argue myself out of what I just felt, which I guess is kind of proving your point in a frustrating way. I'll try to hold onto it, even if some part of me is already waiting for Sunday to prove me wrong.
therapist: The fact that you caught yourself mid-argument and named it out loud — that *is* your track record changing, right here in this room, even if it doesn't feel dramatic enough to count yet. I notice your voice has gone quite quiet, like you're holding something carefully, and I want to honor that — what you're carrying is heavy, and "I'll try to hold onto it" is actually a brave thing to say when part of you is already bracing for disappointment. That willingness to try, even without certainty, is exactly the kind of thing worth bringing with you into Sunday.
vocal_descriptors: very high pitch, very quiet, fast speech
